questions.q: Why isn't a remote backend by itself enough to prevent state corruption?
options: It doesn't stop two people from running apply at nearly the same time and writing to state without coordination
Remote state can only be read, never written
Remote backends don't support the azurerm provider
It requires a VPN connection that most teams don't have
questions.explain: A remote backend solves the shared-copy problem but says nothing about timing — locking is what adds coordination.

questions.q: How does the azurerm backend provide state locking?
options: By requiring manual approval from an Azure admin before every apply
By requiring a separate DynamoDB table, same as the s3 backend
Automatically, using Azure Blob Storage's native lease mechanism, with no extra configuration
It doesn't support locking at all
questions.explain: The azurerm backend gets locking for free through blob leases — nothing extra needs to be set in the backend block.

questions.q: What does the s3 backend need in order to support state locking?
options: A dynamodb_table argument pointing at a DynamoDB table with a LockID primary key of type String
A second S3 bucket dedicated entirely to locks
An IAM role named exactly 'terraform-lock'
Nothing — s3 locks automatically like azurerm does
questions.explain: S3 has no native lease mechanism, so the s3 backend coordinates locks through rows in a DynamoDB table keyed on LockID.

questions.q: What does Terraform do if you run apply while another apply already holds the state lock?
options: It refuses and prints an error identifying who holds the lock, what operation, and when it started
It proceeds anyway and merges both sets of changes
It deletes the existing lock and takes over immediately
It queues your apply silently and runs it automatically once the lock clears
questions.explain: The lock error's Who and Created fields tell you exactly whose operation to wait on before retrying.

questions.q: When is it actually safe to run terraform force-unlock on a held lock?
options: Any time an apply is taking longer than expected
Only the original engineer who created the lock is ever allowed to unlock it
Immediately, since force-unlock is designed for routine use
Only after confirming the operation that holds it isn't actually still running, e.g. a crashed process left it stuck
questions.explain: Forcing an unlock while a real apply is still in flight is exactly the concurrent-write corruption locking exists to prevent.
